Baba's Tongue

The Kidd Workshop — Spring Anthology · 2024

An original poem exploring language, distance, and the inheritance of silence between a daughter and her father.

"If love is a language, then Baba tried / to share his love with me. / Love that was a mouthful / of indiscernible words / and throaty melodies / I couldn't conjure."

Typo

The Kidd Workshop — Spring Anthology · 2024

A meditation on mortality sparked by an accidental search query, tracing the punctuation of life and death.

"I typed into Google today / what dies instead of what does. / A typo, / a careless accident, / a moment of irony after reading an elegy / and living one that isn't yet written, / but life is always foreshadowing its end."

Temporality in Poetry and the Physical Space of Time on the Page

The Kidd Workshop · 2024

A 10-page research paper exploring how temporal experience is encoded through stanzaic form, written during a year-long intensive poetry workshop.

"My fascination with temporality stems from my desire to conquer my fear of time passing and this poem illustrates how gratitude for the present is a grounding practice, which resonated with me. I was particularly taken by the lines 'This is To-day. To-morrow might bring death – /and life the gleeful madrigal of birds,/ be drowned in the glimmer of sleep' (Sassoon, lines 8-10). These beautiful images, combined with the em-dash, render death as an integral part of life. Yet, with the following lines, all of the power of living seems to lie in the appreciation of the present, which conquers the fear of time passing."

Close Reading: Rupert Brooke's "Dining-Room Tea" (1910)

University of Oregon Nomad Journal · 2023

Published in the University of Oregon's Comparative Literature Journal — examining temporality and presence in Brooke's 1910 poem.

"'Dining-Room Tea,' written in 1910, delineates a paradoxical moment when time felt timeless. True to its name, the poem portrays a lively dining room scene in which the narrator, presumably Brooke himself, reflects on watching his loved ones laugh and drink tea together. Though the scene only lasts an instant, in reality, Brooke's concept of time extends the experience beyond its actual duration."
